One should consume one such portion around the second hour, and another around the tenth hour, and they will suffer no harm from hunger. Another composition of the same type uses half a sextarius <note>a Roman unit of measure, approximately half a liter</note> of Attic sesame, half that amount of honey, a cotyla <note>a small liquid measure</note> of oil, and a choenix <note>a dry measure</note> of peeled sweet almonds. You must dry the sesame and grind the almonds, then sift them. Next, peel the squills <note>sea onions</note>, remove the roots and leaves, and chop them into small pieces. Place them in a mortar and crush them until they are thoroughly smoothed. Then, take an equal part of the crushed squills to the honey and work them together evenly with the oil. Pour the mixture into a pot and place it over coals, stirring it continuously with a wooden spatula until everything is combined. When the mass has solidified, it will be worth the effort to divide it into small morsels. By taking one in the morning and another in the evening, a person will have sufficient nourishment. This medicine is useful for an army, for being sweet, it brings satiety and quenches thirst. We have extracted these instructions from a certain manuscript commentary on the book of Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, a mathematician and engineer</note> found in the Vatican Library. We saw the same composition in Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator</note>, in his fifth book on military affairs, where he describes other similar things of this kind.

->*From which fruits wines may be made.*<-

### CHAP. XXI.

Now we shall review the fruits from which wines may be made. First, we consider those made by our ancestors, which fall into two categories: some serve as remedies, with which medical books are filled, while others are for various uses, appearing in nearly infinite varieties depending on the differences between regions and peoples. ->*Wine from palms*<-

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of Natural History</note> stated that wine is made from these in the East, and he enumerates fifty kinds of palms and the differences in the wines derived from them. Among these, the dates are most celebrated, being very rich in juice; from them, the finest wines of the East are produced. These wines are harmful to the head, from which fact the fruit derives its name <note>the Greek word "kara" means head</note>.
